answer:
**Short answer:** The vault doesn't contain Paul Graham saying whether a founder in Stockholm, or anywhere outside the Valley, should move. What it does show is what PG and YC did: when they started YC in Cambridge, Massachusetts, they moved it to Silicon Valley within months. PG has also written that Silicon Valley is unusually good at backing people who failed and learned from it. Those two facts point toward "yes, at least for a while," but that conclusion is my extrapolation, not something PG says in these sources.

**What they've said**
- **PG (2023):** "This is one reason Silicon Valley is so tolerant of failure. People in Silicon Valley aren't blindly tolerant of failure. They'll only continue to bet on you if you're learning from your failures." ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html), 2023). He means that investors there will back a founder again after a failure, which he argues matters because returns in startups compound.
- **Livingston, recounting PG (2024):** after the first summer batch in Cambridge, "Paul said in like September oh we have to do this out in Silicon Valley" ([How YC Was Created @ 21:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=1293s)). This is her account of what PG said, not his own words.
- **Livingston (2018):** "we didn't want someone else to be the Y Combinator of Silicon Valley, we wanted to be that ourselves" ([9 Things She Learned @ 12:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=722s)).

**What they've done**
- They first called the firm "Cambridge Seed," then dropped the name because "we don't want to limit oursel geographically" ([@ 5:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=305s)).
- They moved YC's operations to Silicon Valley "in a matter of months." Livingston says that was only possible because they had stayed small ([@ 25:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1510s)).
- In a 2024 interview, Livingston said PG and she live in England, and that PG gets "a fire hose of startups" when he comes back, because "we don't get a lot of that stimulation in England" ([@ 10:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=608s)).

**Where this is uncertain**
- None of these sources is PG directly advising a founder about where to live. Most of the evidence is Livingston's retelling or YC's own decisions.
- YC moving there doesn't automatically mean every startup should. YC needed to be where the founders and investors were. Your startup might need to be where its users are.
- In the 2024 interview, a Lightcone host contrasts London startup events ("people hanging around… talking about business plans") with YC's batches. That's a host speaking, not a vault member, so I haven't counted it as their view.

**Extrapolation (my reasoning, not something PG says in the vault)**
Here is what PG would probably tell you, built from his documented views:
1. **Go, at least for a stretch.** His idea of superlinear returns says that, for ambitious work, being near the best people and the most investors pays off disproportionately. His failure-tolerance point means a failed attempt in the Valley still leaves you with a reputation investors will bet on again. YC's own move shows he applies this to himself.
2. **Being among peers matters.** YC's batches and weekly dinners are built on founders seeing what other founders are actually shipping and pushing each other. A Stockholm founder can get some of that from YC itself, then decide where to settle.
3. **Make the startup work first.** His recurring advice is to make something people want and grow. He says investors are won over by growth, not by tricks ([[fundraising/convincing-investors/make-the-startup-do-well]]), and the same logic suggests they don't care about your address either. Spotify and Klarna are Stockholm companies, so the city is not a dead end.

**Outside the vault:** PG has written essays about this directly, such as *Cities and Ambition* (2008) and *Why Startups Condense in America* (2006). They aren't in `yc-pre`, so I haven't quoted them. If you want an answer grounded in his actual words, I can add those essays to the vault and re-answer.

**Short answer:** No source in this vault has Paul Graham talking about "brand vs. product" directly. Everything he does say points the same way, though: win on product. To him, competing on brand instead of product is close to "playing house" or "growth hacks", something that might fool investors for a round but won't fool users. The one place he values brand, it's as something that builds up as a side effect of work that's already going well. It isn't a way to compete.

**What they've said**

- **There's no boss to trick, only users.** "There is no boss to trick. ... There's only users. And all users care about is whether your software. Does what they want, right?" ([yt-ii1jcLg-eIQ @ 12:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=730s)). Then: "So, you have to have something people want. And you only prosper to the extent that you do." (@ 12:43)
- **Copying the outward forms is the classic mistake.** Founders who "play house" are "imitating all the outward forms of starting a startup" and neglecting "the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want." ([@ 7:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=452s)). A polished brand on a weak product fits this pattern.
- **Tricks are minor.** "There are tricks in the startups, as there are in any domain. But they are an order of magnitude less important than solving the real problem." ([@ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s))
- **How he thinks growth works:** "The way to make your startup grow is to make something that users really love. Right, and then tell them about it." On growth hacks: "just mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." ([@ 10:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s)). He does make room for marketing, in the "then tell them about it" step. It comes after the product, not in place of it.
- **Faking only hurts the founders.** "Faking does work to some extent with investors." But: "You're playing a confidence trick on yourself. You're wasting your own time, because the startup is doomed." ([@ 12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=763s))
- **Where brand does count for him (2023):** he lists it as something that compounds. Work "can compound directly... when you're building infrastructure, or growing an audience or brand" ([Superlinear Returns](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)). That is brand as a payoff that grows over time. He doesn't present it as a strategy you could use instead of a good product.
- **How a newcomer beats an incumbent:** by being better. "If a company makes a product that people dislike yet still buy, then presumably they'd buy a better alternative if you made one." He adds that when something mediocre stays popular, "there's often a hidden reason why", such as a monopoly or regulation (same essay).
- **Other YC partners:** Seibel and Caldwell (2022) credit Stripe's "really clever brand promise or marketing stance", which was building "the most beautiful website they could with the most beautiful documentation". Even there, the brand was a promise about the product, made to developers ([yt-Jcuqq48CNj8 @ 14:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=886s); the transcript doesn't make clear which of them said it). Livingston (2018): "Focus on making something people want. Everything follows from that." ([yt-8d-cApFHjeY @ 24:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1476s))

**Where this is uncertain**
- The vault has nothing from PG on consumer categories where products are close to identical and brand really does decide the winner (fashion, drinks, cosmetics). His arguments come from software startups.
- The "gaming the system" material is from a 2014 talk to Stanford students, and the YC examples are survivors (Stripe, Airbnb).

**Extrapolation** (not in the sources; reasoned from the principles above)
If a founder told PG "our product is about as good as theirs, so we'll win on brand," he would probably treat it as a warning sign. It would suggest they haven't found anything people badly want, and that they're picking a startup trick over "solving the real problem." He would probably send them back to his test of whether the product is clearly better than a mediocre incumbent. If it isn't, branding won't save it, and if it is, users will spread the word. He'd likely accept brand as (a) a promise about the product, as with Stripe's docs, and (b) something that compounds once the product works. He would not accept it as a substitute in the early stage. This rests on the "playing house", "growth hacks" and "seek work that compounds" principles cited above.

One note of my own: in some consumer categories, brand really is a large part of what customers are buying. This vault doesn't cover PG's view on those.

**Short answer:** The vault can't answer this. Sam Altman is listed as a member of `yc-pre`, but none of its 12 sources contain anything he said. Nothing in the vault records his views on AI, so I can't say which AI future worries him most.

**What's in the vault about him**
Only other people talking about him, and none of it is about AI:
- Jessica Livingston (2024): "Sam Altman was impressive at age 19." ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY @ 54:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY&t=1474s))
- Livingston says YC funded him in its first batch. PG had suggested he wait a year, and he replied "I'm a sophomore and I'm coming." (same video @ 55:08)
- A 2018 Livingston talk mentions his "geolocation startup" in that first batch (`yt-8d-cApFHjeY`).

**Where this is uncertain:** It's all uncertain, because there are no Altman sources at all. The vault's channels and searches have so far turned up content by PG, Livingston, Seibel, Caldwell and Tan.

**Extrapolation** (labelled)
I can't build a real extrapolation for Altman. There are no documented principles of his to reason from, and I won't borrow another member's view and present it as his.

The closest thing in the vault is another member's worry about AI: **Paul Graham's**, not Altman's. In *Writes and Write-Nots* (2024), PG fears a future where AI does people's writing and so most of them stop thinking: "So a world divided into writes and write-nots is more dangerous than it sounds. It will be a world of thinks and think-nots." ([paulgraham.com/writes.html](https://paulgraham.com/writes.html)) Treat this as YC-adjacent context only. Nothing in the vault suggests Altman holds this view.

**To actually answer this:** add Altman's own material to the vault (his blog at blog.samaltman.com, his CS183B lectures, interviews on the YC channel), then curate, fetch and compile it. If you want, I can add those sources to `vault.yaml` and run discovery.

**Short answer:** The vault doesn't have a talk where Seibel covers fundraising directly. Going by what he has said, he would call months of deck polishing and follow-up meetings time not spent on the one thing that matters: putting a product in front of real customers. Investor enthusiasm, or the lack of it, is a weak signal next to that.

**What he's said**

- **A deck is worth less than a product.** "So spending all that time on a pitch deck is not as valuable as spending your time building anything that you can give to a customer." ([Startup School 2019 @ 11:11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=671s))
- **The early job is launching, getting customers and iterating.** He says "launch something bad quickly" is the one thing to take away, and that "the second thing that an early stage startup needs to do is get some initial customers. Get anyone using your product." ([@ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)) He also warns: "You'd be surprised at how many founders journeys end before a single user has actually interacted with a product they've created." ([@ 2:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=134s))
- **He mocks founders who let investors steer the plan.** You "talk to an investor and they say, 'Oh, that could never be a company.' Because investors know everything." Then a three-week plan "turns into a three-month plan." ([@ 11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=704s)) He's being sarcastic: investor opinions shouldn't move your plan.
- **Investor rejection says little about the idea.** Coinbase "had a impossible time raising money on demo day and so if he had taken the demo day signal, the investor signal of 'oh we don't want to give you money', and quit, we don't have Coinbase." ([Seibel & Caldwell 2022 @ 12:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=723s); the transcript has no speaker labels, so attributing this to Seibel is medium confidence.) His rule is to ignore "experts" who don't like the idea, "especially if they're not going to be users" ([@ 19:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1182s)).
- **Products win, not whiteboard strategy.** "We can't, you know, talk on a whiteboard and plan our strategy and win. All of these founders had to actually do [it]" and "build good products" ([@ 18:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=1116s)).

**Same view from PG (YC 2014, not Seibel):** "The best way to convince investors, is to start a startup that's actually doing well, meaning growing fast, and then simply tell investors so." ([Stanford CS183B @ 9:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=591s)) He adds that someone who "knows zero about fund raising but has made something users really love will have an easier time raising money" than someone with "every trick in the book, but has a flat usage graph" ([@ 13:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=797s)).

**Where this is uncertain**

- The vault has no Seibel talk about fundraising as such: rounds, valuations, how long a raise should take, how to run a process. Everything above comes from his MVP and startup-ideas talks.
- His examples are billion-dollar survivors (Airbnb, Coinbase, Stripe). They don't show how often the investors who passed were right.
- I don't know your traction. If you already have users and growth, the points about "go build instead" weigh less, and the useful question becomes why that growth isn't converting into a round.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not his words)

1. **Months of pitching is a symptom.** If the raise is dragging, he'd probably first ask whether you have users and whether they're growing. If not, the deck isn't the bottleneck. The launch-fast, get-customers, iterate loop is ([[launch-quickly]], [[make-the-startup-do-well]]).
2. **Stop polishing and ship.** By his deck-vs-product line, each extra week on slides is a week not spent putting something in front of customers. Cut back pitching and spend that time on users.
3. **Follow-up meetings aren't progress.** Applying his "investors know everything" sarcasm: don't count meetings as traction, and don't change your product to fit investor feedback.
4. **Rejections aren't a verdict, but they aren't a reason to keep pitching either.** The Coinbase story says don't quit because investors passed. Taken with PG's point, the answer is to keep building until the numbers make the pitch easy, not to keep pitching.

One note from me: this applies most to software and consumer products. Seibel himself allows a "heavy MVP" for regulated or hard-tech companies, where you may truly need capital before you can ship anything. In that case the pitching may be necessary, and his advice here fits less well.

**Short answer:** Nothing in the vault has Dalton Caldwell taking up "modest and safe vs. ambitious" head-on. What he did say points against the idea that you can pick a safe one. In his telling, YC's biggest wins (Airbnb, Coinbase, Stripe) looked like bad, risky or second-rate ideas when they started, and the founders themselves underestimated how big they were. "Looks safe" and "looks bad" aren't reliable signals either way.

**What he's said** (all from "Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From?", YC, 2022, co-hosted with Michael Seibel: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8)
- **His own first read was wrong.** He saw Airbnb as "the third-rate entrant to a crowded space at the time" ([@ 1:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=98s)). Renting a room with the host present was "the ultimate unappealing, scary, bad thing that no one wanted to do" (@ 4:57).
- **The conventional wisdom of the time was wrong too.** Charging for a community was "seen as uncool and impure" (@ 5:30), and "the third-rate knock-off version of something actually good was what YC companies were" (@ 18:03, medium confidence).
- **Founders aim too low, not too high.** Even Brian Armstrong "didn't really believe in his own idea" in his YC application. "The simple promise of buying bitcoin in a non-sketchy way with a debit card in the US … That was enough" ([@ 10:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=656s), medium confidence).
- **Hard problems are where the openings are.** Getting a merchant account before Stripe "was like applying for a mortgage" (@ 12:34). Building payments was "gnarly and the opposite of easy in every way" ([@ 13:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=788s)), and Stripe took it on anyway.

Seibel's closing advice in the same talk, which Caldwell was co-presenting: ignore experts who think it's a bad idea, especially if they'd never use the product. Be careful with your early estimates of market size, and "don't be discouraged if someone's like, that's a tiny market" (@ 19:42–20:16, medium confidence).

**What he's done:** He's a repeat founder (at least three companies). He used the bad products that came before Airbnb (VRBO) and Stripe (pre-Stripe merchant accounts). He also passed on Bitcoin in 2011 because buying it "seemed too much like a total scam" (@ 7:42). So he openly counts himself among the people who misjudged these ideas.

**Where this is uncertain**
- The talk only looks at three of YC's biggest winners after the fact. It says nothing about how many ambitious, bad-looking ideas failed. That's a real gap if you're asking about *odds*.
- The video transcript doesn't say who's talking, so several of the lines above are attributed to Caldwell with medium confidence.
- Paul Graham, also in this vault, gives a counterweight: "Exposing oneself to superlinear returns is not for everyone" (Superlinear Returns, 2023).

**Extrapolation** (not something he's said; reasoned from the points above)
Caldwell would probably push back on the framing. In his examples, the ideas that looked safe and modest were the knock-offs in crowded spaces, and the winners looked scary, uncool or tiny. So choosing for safety probably just means choosing by the same outside opinion he says was wrong. His actual test is different. Is there an existing product that's bad and that you or your friends have used and hated? Can you make something 10x better? Are you willing to do the "gnarly" part? A small-looking idea that passes that test is fine, since he'd expect it to turn out bigger than you think, as Coinbase did. A "safe" idea picked only because it seems low-risk, with no real pain behind it, is the one he'd be skeptical of.

My own view, separate from his: he's right that "looks safe" doesn't mean "is safe." But the survivorship gap is real, and this talk can't tell you whether ambitious ideas actually have better odds.

**Short answer:** The vault has nothing from Garry Tan on this. It contains no statement from him about AI agents, skill files, or who owns work you do for an employer. His only material is host lines from a 2024 Lightcone episode about YC's history. The closest thing in the vault comes from Paul Graham, not Tan: he says your work should be something you carry from job to job. So by that YC logic, ownership matters.

**What Tan has said in the vault**
- Nothing on this topic. Tan has one source, the Lightcone interview with Jessica Livingston ([yt-6u4JVz7iQTY](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6u4JVz7iQTY)). In it he talks about Posterous ("I just wanted you to fund my startup posterous which you did", @ 42:09) and his fund, Initialized (@ 40:30). He says nothing about AI tools, ownership or employment.
- The vault is "pre-2026," so anything Tan said recently about agents isn't in it. I'm not going to fill that gap from memory.

**What the vault does have (PG, not Tan)**

In *Superlinear Returns* (2023, [paulgraham.com/superlinear.html](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html)):
- "Not to equate work with a job." … "For someone like that, their work is something they carry with them from job to job, if they have jobs at all." ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]]; by: pg)
- "Seek work that compounds … when you're building infrastructure, or growing an audience or brand. Or work can compound by teaching you, since learning compounds." ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]]; by: pg)
- On his own past, he says that "artists seemed least at the mercy of organizations" ([[web-76d87c7c2e80]]; by: pg).

In *When To Do What You Love* (2024, [paulgraham.com/when.html](https://paulgraham.com/when.html)):
- "You don't necessarily need a job doing x in order to work on x; often you can just start doing it in some form yourself." ([[web-7254f259673a]]; by: pg)

**Where this is uncertain**
- PG's line is about *your work* in the sense of skills and judgment, not files or IP. He never discusses employment contracts or who legally owns code.
- Tan is a different person from PG. Nothing in the vault shows whether Tan agrees with PG here.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from YC-group principles, not anything Tan said)
- On PG's compounding test, a library of agent workflows and skills is infrastructure that compounds. If it stays locked in your employer's repo when you leave, it stops compounding *for you*. The YC view would be that this matters.
- The part you can always take with you is what you learned: how you break tasks down for agents and which prompts and structures work. PG's "learning compounds" says that's the bigger asset anyway.
- In practice, that suggests building general-purpose patterns on your own time and your own machines, in some form you control ("start doing it in some form yourself"). Keep the employer-specific versions at work. This isn't legal advice: your employment agreement decides who owns what you build on the job.
- If Tan has views here, they'd probably come from his recent material on AI-native companies, and that isn't in this vault.

If you want a grounded answer about Tan specifically, I can add his YouTube channel or recent Lightcone episodes to a newer vault and search those.

**Short answer:** No. Michael Seibel's advice is the opposite: launch something bad now, to a small set of users, and fix only their biggest problems. Building everything before launch is the trap he warns about. The vault has nothing from Dalton Caldwell on launching or MVPs, so his part below is thin.

**What Michael Seibel has said** (2019 Startup School talk, "How to Plan an MVP": https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM)
- **Launch something bad quickly.** He calls this the one thing to take away: "If you can walk away from one thing from this presentation, it's launch something bad quickly." ([@ 1:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=101s)) He also defines launch loosely: "How about launch is when you get any customers." ([@ 10:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=607s))
- **Weeks, not months.** "You should be able to build it fast in weeks, not months." ([@ 4:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=269s)) At 3 months in, you're already past his window.
- **Small set of users, their top problems, ignore the rest.** "They should just focus on a small set of initial users and their highest order problems and then ignore the rest until later." ([@ 5:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=303s)) That answers the request pile: most requests go in "later."
- **Cut the spec, including important things.** "Just cut the stuff that clearly isn't important. Um, and if there's no non-important things, start cutting important things." ([@ 12:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=737s)) He describes your situation exactly: "your three-week plan turns into a three-month plan." ([@ 11:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=704s))
- **Not launching becomes a habit.** "If you don't have anything out in the world, it's very easy to just delay, delay, delay, delay." ([@ 12:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=771s)) He adds: "You'd be surprised at how many founders journeys end before a single user has actually interacted with a product they've created." ([@ 2:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=134s))
- **Don't fall in love with what you built.** "It might turn out the full thing that you want to build isn't what your customers want at all." He also says: "Hold the problem you're solving tightly, hold the customer tightly, hold the solution you're building loosely." ([@ 3:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=199s))
- **Talk to users after launch, not only before.** "It's a lot harder to learn from your customers when they don't have a product they can play with." ([@ 10:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=639s))

**What Dalton Caldwell has said:** The vault has only one Caldwell source: a 2022 talk with Seibel about where startup ideas come from (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8). It doesn't cover feature scope or launch timing. The closest point comes from Seibel in that talk: Airbnb launched without payments, and the founders found that gap by using their own product ([@ 4:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=264s)). In other words, you don't need every insight before launch, because real use shows you what's missing.

**What they've done:** Seibel's examples were all thin at launch. Airbnb had no payments and no map view. Justin.tv, his own company, had one channel. Stripe had "almost no features", and the founders integrated it for customers by hand ([@ 7:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=438s)).

**Where this is uncertain**
- No source in the vault covers how to handle a growing list of feature requests from people who aren't using a live product yet, or how AI coding tools change the cost of building. The 2019 talk predates Claude Code.
- His one exception is a "heavy MVP" for regulated or hard-tech work like banking, insurance or rockets. Even then he says to start with a simple website ([@ 8:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1hHMwLxN6EM&t=539s)).
- The profile notes that his examples are billion-dollar survivors, and that "launch quickly" is YC's house view rather than tested advice.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from his principles, not something either of them said)
- **Cheap building doesn't change the rule.** Seibel's argument is about learning, not engineering cost: you can't tell if a product solves a problem until people use it. If Claude Code lets you build 10x faster, he'd likely say that makes the risk worse. Each feature built for a request on a call is a guess about what people will do, made by someone who has never used the product. "Weeks not months" is about how long you go without that feedback, not how long the code takes.
- **The request pile is a symptom.** Requests from calls tell you what people *say* they want. His framework puts what they *do* with a live product above that. He'd likely tell you to stop building, pick the one user (or few) with the most painful problem, cut the product down to what solves that, and get it in their hands this week. "Launch" means they're using it, not a press launch. Their requests after they've used it count far more than requests from calls before.
- **A rough test:** if a requested feature isn't blocking your first users' biggest problem, it goes on the "later" list, however easy it is to build.
- **Caldwell:** From his talk, he'd probably ask whether these users are desperate for the product or just giving polite wishlists. In that talk, Seibel gives the test for a real insight: people want it badly even when it's the most expensive option on the market. A long list of feature requests from people who haven't used the product doesn't pass that test.

My own view: I'd agree with the extrapolation. Fast AI-assisted building makes it easier to postpone launching, not less risky.

**Short answer:** Nothing in the vault has Michael Seibel talking about cofounder breakups, vesting disputes or lawyers. The only sources from him are about MVPs and startup ideas. The closest material is from Jessica Livingston, who spent years mediating cofounder disputes at YC. Her views, plus Seibel's habit of putting speed ahead of process, point one way: settle quickly and cheaply, and stop paying lawyers to fight over equity in a company that has no value yet.

**What they've said (grounded)**

- **Livingston: helping cofounders through disputes and breakups was part of her job at YC.** "I'd counsel them on relationships that were under strained due to the pressure of a start-up and I'd listen at length and help them with their co-founder disputes and breakups starting a startup is emotionally draining for founders especially in the beginning" ([2018 talk @ 18:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1098s); by: livingston; conf: high). She treats a breakup as a normal, survivable part of early startups, not a scandal.
- **Livingston: be blunt with each other.** She says she tried "to always be a straight shooter with my advice", and that PG doesn't "withhold the truth in order to preserve people's feelings" ([@ 18:18–18:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1098s)).
- **Livingston: squeezing a small outcome makes no sense.** She tells of a failing husband-and-wife startup. PG helped them land the jobs they wanted, and an investor who had hoped for an acqui-hire was furious. She concludes: "to this day I still don't get why investors squeeze founders over small outcomes like this" ([@ 20:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1236s)). YC was "benevolent to failing startups" ([@ 19:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1166s)). She's talking about investors there, not cofounders, but the principle fits your situation.
- **Livingston: what to screen for next time.** "Find a co-founder with complimentary skills but the same moral compass as you". She and PG "agreed on the big questions and we each deferred to each other's expertise on the small ones" ([@ 23:59–24:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=1439s)). When judging applicants, the thing she cared about most was "what was the relationship between the co-founders like?" ([@ 14:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=891s)).

**What they've done:** Livingston set up YC's standard legal paperwork for founders ([@ 13:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-cApFHjeY&t=793s)). The goal was to make startup legal work standard and cheap, not something to negotiate from scratch.

**Where this is uncertain:** The vault has only two sources from Seibel: *How to Plan an MVP* (2019) and *Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From?* (2022, with Dalton Caldwell). Neither touches cofounder conflict, equity or legal disputes, and the vault's profile doesn't list cofounder relationships as one of his areas. He has very likely covered this elsewhere, but those talks aren't in the vault, so I can't cite them. Livingston's advice is about mediating and choosing cofounders. She never says how to split vested stock.

**Extrapolation (not in any source; my reasoning from their stated principles)**

1. **Work out what the fight is about.** Nine months in and before product-market fit, the equity is probably worth very little today. Every round of lawyer letters spends real cash and months of attention fighting over a share of something close to zero. This follows from Livingston's "why squeeze small outcomes" and from Seibel's general impatience with anything that isn't building for users.
2. **Talk directly and settle it fast.** In the spirit of "straight shooter", the two of you should meet without lawyers and agree on terms. Let the lawyers write up what you agreed instead of negotiating for you.
3. **The vested stock is his.** That's what vesting is for. Pushing to take back vested shares is the kind of squeeze Livingston criticizes. The usual YC-style resolution is that he keeps his vested shares and the unvested ones go back to the company. If you're continuing the company, ask for the things that actually matter: he signs IP assignment, gives you a proxy or voting agreement so a departed holder can't block future rounds, and you both sign mutual releases. If you're shutting down, it doesn't matter who holds the stock.
4. **Decide whether the company continues.** If neither of you would keep working on it, wind it down cleanly and move on. If you would, the bigger risk is wasting six months on this dispute instead of finding product-market fit.
5. **Next time, screen for the relationship.** Pick a cofounder with the same moral compass, and before you start, agree on how a breakup would work: vesting, a cliff and what happens on departure.

One line of my own: I'm not a lawyer, and none of this is legal advice. Your jurisdiction, cap table, any investors and the wording of your vesting agreement all matter, so get your lawyer to approve whatever the two of you agree.

5. **Treat what you notice as possible startup ideas.** Paul Graham says that at the leading edge "you'll know they're something that ought to exist" (@ 29:06). When an agent fails at a task in your industry, write it down. That gap may be a product.

**Short answer:** The vault has nothing from PG about AI agents, agent payments or payments infrastructure. What it does have is his general rules for judging startups, and those point to questions he'd likely ask: who is actually using this today and wants it badly, is it growing, and are you building it because you live in the future or because it sounds like a big trend?

**What PG has said that applies**

- **Make something people want; anything else is playing house.** He warns about founders who copy "all the outward forms of starting a startup" while they "neglected the one thing that's actually essential which is to make something people want." "There is no boss to trick. ... There's only users." ([2014 Stanford lecture](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=452s) @ 7:32, [@ 12:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=730s))
- **Ideas you thought up on purpose are suspect.** "If you make a conscious effort to try and think of startup ideas, you will think of ideas that are not only bad, but bad and plausible sounding." The good ones come from getting "to the leading edge of some technology, to... live in the future." ([@ 24:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1474s), [@ 29:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=1746s))
- **Know your users, not startups.** "What you need is expertise in your own users." ([@ 5:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=347s))
- **Watch the growth rate, and do things that don't scale.** "If you pay a ridiculous amount of attention to your tiny initial set of customers, ideally you'll kick off exponential growth by word of mouth." Also: "In a market with network effects, a company that grows fast enough can shut out potential competitors." ([Superlinear Returns, 2023](https://paulgraham.com/superlinear.html))
- **Mediocre incumbents often survive for a hidden reason.** "When something is popular despite being mediocre, there's often a hidden reason why. Perhaps monopoly or regulation make it hard to compete. Perhaps customers have bad taste or have broken procedures for deciding what to buy." (same essay)
- **Growth hacks:** "mentally translate it in your mind to bullshit." ([@ 10:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ii1jcLg-eIQ&t=626s))

The payments lessons in the vault come from **Seibel and Caldwell, not PG**. Stripe started from a problem its founders watched their YC peers have ("If all of your smart technical friends are complaining about the same thing, maybe it's a real problem," Seibel), and it "went nuts at making something that developers would just freak out about" (Caldwell) ([2022 ideas talk](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jcuqq48CNj8&t=854s) @ 14:14, @ 15:18).

**Where this is uncertain:** Most of the PG material here is from 2014 to 2025 and none of it is about AI agents. He said in 2024 he is "usually reluctant to make predictions about technology." The vault's PG sources are mostly essays, not office-hours transcripts, so his questioning style itself is inferred.

**Extrapolation** (my reasoning from the principles above, not things PG has said)

1. **"Who used it this week, and what did they buy?"** He'd want a specific agent, built by a specific team, completing real purchases. A diagram of the agent economy wouldn't count. If your users are hypothetical agents that don't exist yet, that's playing house.
2. **"Are you building this because you hit the problem yourselves?"** Did you build agents that got stuck at a checkout? Or did you read that agentic commerce will be huge? The second is a "bad and plausible sounding" idea, and this one sounds very plausible right now, which would make him more suspicious.
3. **"Which side are you serving first?"** You have three groups to win: agent developers, merchants and card networks or issuers. He'd push you to pick one narrow group you can serve obsessively. Stripe's equivalent was developers integrating by hand.
4. **"Why hasn't this been solved already?"** His hidden-reason heuristic applies directly: card network rules, fraud and chargeback liability, KYC, merchants' bot blocking. He'd want to know whether you see the real obstacle and have a way through it. A nicer API on top doesn't count.
5. **"What's your weekly growth rate?"** He'd ask for completed transactions or active agent integrations, measured week over week. Pilots, LOIs and partnership announcements wouldn't count.
6. **"What happens when OpenAI, Stripe or Visa ships this?"** Applying the network-effects line: is there a loop where each merchant makes you more useful to agents, and each agent more useful to merchants? If so, how fast can you grow so you get there first?

My own view, separate from PG: question 4 is probably the most important one for payments infrastructure in particular, because liability and network rules usually decide who wins.
